analysis.one_liner: Replaces state accident-liability rules for small aircraft with uniform federal standards, including a time cutoff on claims against manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill won 162 bipartisan cosponsors and passed the House Transportation Committee, but never received a House vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have moved lawsuits over small-plane crashes out of the 50 different state legal systems and into one set of federal rules. Those rules would have cut off most claims against aircraft manufacturers 12 years after a plane was first sold, limited when punitive damages are available, shortened the deadline for filing a lawsuit to two years, and allowed defendants to move cases from state to federal court. The stated goal was to ease rising product-liability costs that the bill's findings said were pushing small-aircraft makers out of the market.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of small planes, engines, and parts, along with their liability insurers, would gain the most: a 12-year cutoff would end their exposure to claims about older aircraft, FAA compliance would count as evidence against defect claims, and punitive damages would require a high proof standard. Owners and operators would also see their exposure trimmed by the shorter filing deadlines. Plaintiffs who win would get faster, more uniform awards under comparative-fault rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a 12-year limit on suits against aircraft manufacturers, counting from the plane's first delivery or a part's replacement, after which no claim could be brought [S2][S3].
It applies uniform federal principles of comparative responsibility and, for most defendants, several rather than joint liability, so a manufacturer pays only its proportional share [S2][S3].

Evidence that a product complied with Federal Aviation Administration standards would be admissible to argue it was not defective, and manufacturers would escape liability if an FAA airworthiness directive could have corrected the flaw [S3].

Punitive damages would be available only on clear and convincing proof of conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and defendants' financial information would be kept out of evidence until a plaintiff made that preliminary showing [S2][S3].
All such cases could be filed in or removed to federal district courts, and the bill states that Congress intends Rule 11 sanctions against frivolous filings to be strictly enforced [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Victims of small-plane crashes and their families would bear the cost. Anyone harmed by an aircraft or part more than 12 years old would lose the right to sue the manufacturer, even for a proven defect, and all plaintiffs would face a two-year filing deadline that preempts longer state deadlines. Where a defendant is insolvent or underinsured, a plaintiff left with only proportional (several) liability recoveries could go uncompensated.

drawbacks.text: The 12-year cutoff is absolute for aircraft built to a 40-year useful life; a defect victim in year 13 would recover nothing from the manufacturer regardless of how strong the case was [S3].

Replacing joint liability with several liability means a plaintiff hurt by multiple defective components could collect only each defendant's percentage share, leaving the shortfall uncompensated if another defendant cannot pay; the bill itself orders a Transportation Department study of whether awarded damages go uncollected [S2][S3].
The bill preempts state damage-recovery law, overriding stronger state consumer-protection rules, and adds a strict two-year filing deadline with service required within 120 days [S3].
Strict enforcement of Rule 11 sanctions, including attorney's fees, would raise the risk for plaintiffs' lawyers of bringing close cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered manufacturers and insurers genuine relief from long-tail liability, and its findings cite real evidence that liability costs were pushing makers out of the small-plane market. But the design of the trade was one-sided: the protections for industry were firm and immediate, while the protections for victims — the uncollectible-damages study, the express-warranty exception, the duty to keep issuing safety warnings — were secondary, and the 12-year cutoff would wipe out valid claims outright. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the people most hurt by defective older aircraft are exactly the people the cutoff leaves with no remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House committee in August 1989, but no floor vote ever came, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 8, 1989 and referred the same day to three committees: Public Works and Transportation, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
It gathered 162 cosponsors — 100 of the chamber's 175 Republicans and 62 of its 257 Democrats — an unusually broad bipartisan base [S4].
The Aviation Subcommittee held hearings on May 24, 1989 and forwarded the bill to the full committee on July 18 [S5].
The Public Works and Transportation Committee amended the bill in markup on July 20 and reported it on August 4, 1989 (H. Rept. 101-218, Part I) [S5].
No further action appears in the record: neither of the other two referred committees reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crash victims and their families came out ahead, because the state-law rights to sue aircraft makers that the bill would have cut off stayed intact. Small-aircraft manufacturers and their insurers, despite the committee win, got none of the liability limits they sought; the industry's version of this idea did not become law until years later in a different Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crash victims kept their right to sue

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan in cosponsorship — 100 of 175 Republicans and 62 of 257 Democrats signed on — but the bill stalled in the Democratically controlled House without a floor vote.

industries.note: The 12-year cutoff, FAA-compliance evidence, and punitive-damages limits would sharply reduce their liability exposure and insurance costs. The gain comes directly out of crash victims' ability to recover from makers of older aircraft.
Ending claims on aircraft older than 12 years and capping damages theories would shrink long-tail exposure for the insurers writing product-liability policies for the industry.

A stricter federal framework, limited punitive damages, short filing deadlines, and strict Rule 11 sanctions would shrink the pool of viable cases and their fee base. Their interest in this bill ran alongside injured clients' ability to recover.

industries.industry: Small-aircraft owners, operators, and repair shops
industries.note: The bill's rules apply to them as defendants too, so shorter deadlines and federal removal would cut their exposure, but they would remain liable for negligence. The bill also orders a study of whether damages from owners, operators, and mechanics go uncollected.
